title: B008: False positive for frozen dataclass defaults with immutable fields
body:
### Summary

B008 flags frozen dataclass constructors used as default values for function parameters, even when all fields contain immutable values. 
Example:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Foo:
    val: bool = True

def bar(foo: Foo = Foo()) -> None: ...
```

Instances of frozen dataclasses whose fields contain only immutable values can safely be shared as default arguments, as fields cannot be reassigned and their contents cannot be mutated, so using such instances as defaults does not present a shared-mutation risk. 
In general `frozen=True` provides only shallow immutability, so exempting every frozen dataclass would be too broad, but could Ruff recognize cases where all fields have immutable types and defaults? `extend-immutable-calls` provides a workaround, but requires manually registering an immutable class. 
Related discussion: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/discussions/19526

label: linter
title: Support `flake8-lazy` style relative import in `__lazy_modules__`
body:
### Summary

The names inside `__lazy_modules__` always have to be absolute, so in order to make a relative import lazy, you need to put the corresponding absolute import into `__lazy_modules__` which breaks symmetry.

While ruff is generally aware of a project's structure when linting it, so relative imports can easily be mapped to absolute ones, this is not as much the case with flake8 or any of its plugins. While it's certainly possible to add similar project detection and configuration options into a flake8 plugin, it's far from economical to do this and generally a bad idea for a plugin. flake8 would need to add those capabilities itself, which seems unlikely to ever happen.

As a result [`flake8-lazy`](https://github.com/henryiii/flake8-lazy/) chose to support a specific style of f-string generated lazy imports. `flake8-type-checking` [plans to support this style as well](https://github.com/snok/flake8-type-checking/pull/211/commits/604e4cca0c75ae7a02131c0f0704b7966dabfe1e):

```python
__lazy_modules__ = [
    # matches .lazy
    f"{__spec__.parent}.lazy",
    # matches ..lazy, but type checkers will complain, since `parent` is `str | None`, so `rsplit` might raise.
    f"{__spec__.parent.rsplit('.', 1)[0]}.lazy",
    # matches ...lazy and is type safe
    f"{(__spec__.parent or '').rsplit('.', 2)[0]}.lazy"
]
```

So we can continue to use ruff and certain flake8 plugins side-by-side I think it's a good idea for ruff to support this style at least at the detection level. I have no strong opinion about whether ruff should ever suggest generating a relative lazy import like that. I can certainly see arguments for it, like also making it easier to tell for humans which lines in `__lazy_modules__` map to relative imports, but also arguments against it, such as aesthetics.

label: formatter
title: Formatter changes the value of implicitly concatenated strings when joining after an octal escape
body:
### Summary

When `ruff format` joins implicitly concatenated string or bytes literals into one literal, an octal escape at the end of one part can absorb leading octal digits of the next part. This changes the runtime value of the literal.

```python
# octal.py
x = b"A\0" b"1\0"
y = "\1" "2"
print(x, repr(y))
```

```console
$ python octal.py
b'A\x001\x00' '\x012'
$ ruff format --isolated octal.py
1 file reformatted
$ cat octal.py
x = b"A\01\0"
y = "\12"
print(x, repr(y))
$ python octal.py
b'A\x01\x00' '\n'
```

`b"A\0" b"1\0"` becomes `b"A\01\0"`, which is a different value. The same happens with `str` literals: `"\1" "2"` becomes `"\12"`, which is `"\n"`.

The trigger is a part that ends with a one- or two-digit octal escape (`\0`, `\1`, `\12`, …) followed by a part that starts with an octal digit `0`–`7`. CPython resolves the escapes in each part before it concatenates them, so the joined text is parsed differently.

The linter had the same problem in the ISC001 fix, which #12936 fixed. The formatter's joining of implicitly concatenated strings seems to still have it.

Expected behavior: either leave such parts unjoined, or pad the escape to three digits when joining (`b"A\0001\0"`, `"\0012"`). Both keep the value.

We found this while checking that a one-off `ruff format` pass over a codebase changed formatting only. It showed up because we compared the AST before and after the pass.

### Version

ruff 0.15.18 (6686f6340 2026-06-18); also reproduced with ruff 0.16.8

title: [rule] Mixing attribute docstrings and doc comments
body:
### Summary

**Background**

Attribute docstrings are a string literal _after_ an assignment, e.g.
```
self.dog = get_snowball()
"""Initialized to snowball"""
```

Sphinx has its own, special syntax called [doc comments](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/extensions/autodoc.html#doc-comments-and-docstrings) with specially formatted comments:
```
#: doc comments precede if at the same indentation level
self.dog = get_snowball()

self.hog = get_babe()  #: but they can also be inline
```

**Proposal**
I am going to assert that if a project uses attribute comments they've standardized on one format or the other. It would be helpful if there was a lint that could enforce their style choice.

**Discussion**
Attribute docstrings have some amount of support in the Python community: there were PEPs 224 and 727 (both rejected). Sphinx, Pyright and Jedi all have support for attribute docstrings. Issue #10347 in this repo has moderate community approval. The doc comments syntax, however, is only supported by Sphinx, and I don't think it has broad community use at all. There's an argument for using attribute docstrings as a default if a default has to be chosen.

Personally, I had no idea doc comments were even a thing, I thought they were LLM hallucinations. I don't know if I've ever seen them in use in an open source project. There's an argument to be made that they should be considered obsolete and rejected on sight.

**Uses**
The lint prevents documentation rendering bugs if a project with doc comments switches away from Sphinx without converting all comments to strings. It could also be used to drive a project-wide migration from one format to the other. A project that's settled on one choice can use the lint to keep the other type from creeping back into a codebase. And if you consider doc comments to be a bug it'll keep them out of your project.

### Summary

PEP 758 / Python 3.14 support `except A, B` syntax for exceptions.

What we have found very consistently from real-world experience is that LLMs get tripped up on this, even when we prominently highlight this as a project convention in places like AGENTS.md + CLAUDE.md. AI/LLM code reviews consistently return the false-positive finding that exception syntax in use for the project is "Python 2 only" when in reality it is valid Python 3.14 syntax.

title: Rules to enforce either doc comments or docstrings for variables/attributes
body:
### Summary

#### Background

There are two distinct conventions in Python for attaching documentation to module-level variables and class attributes:

1. A docstring directly below, e.g.:
    ```python
    name: str
    """
    The user's full name.

    Should not include middle names.
    """
    ```

2. A `#:`[^1] [doc comment](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/extensions/autodoc.html#doc-comments-and-docstrings) directly above, e.g.:
    ```python
    #: The user's full name
    #:
    #: Should not include middle names.
    name: str
    ```

I believe the docstring-below approach (1) is more common nowadays.

The doc-comment-above approach (2) was (according to an LLM's recollections) originally introduced by [epydoc](https://epydoc.sourceforge.net/epydoc.html#variable-docstrings) and then adopted by Sphinx.

#### Rule suggestion

It would be nice if there were rules to enforce either one of these approaches, complaining if the other one is used for a variable/attribute.

If you don't want to implement a rule to enforce doc comments because they seem kind of outdated anyway, it would also be fine to only have a rule that enforces docstrings and complains about doc comments.

[^1]: Spelled out so people may find this issue more easily: *hash colon*

title: Add an extended version of TRY401 for all log levels
body:
### Summary

[TRY401](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/verbose-log-message/) description reads:

> When logging exceptions via `logging.exception`, the exception object is logged automatically. Including the exception object in the log message is redundant and can lead to excessive logging.

I would like to propose an extension of this rule that covers all log levels and logging methods. It should probably be a separate rule and not a configuration flag for TRY401, because the motivation is different.

Pitch: there are popular monitoring solutions such as Sentry that report logs (usually warning and above, or error and above, by default, and configurable by the user) and aggregate them. Including exception object in the log string blocks such aggregation (e.g. `KeyError` returns the missing key in its string representation) and is really _not_ helpful - if exception info is relevant, it's better served by `exc_info=True` instead. This rule should not be enabled by default and should not be autofixable.

Example of violating code:

```python
try:
    1/0
except ZeroDivisionError as exc:
    logger.warning(f"Too many zeros floating around: {exc}")
```

Example of correct code:

```python
try:
    1/0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    logger.warning("Too many zeros floating around")

try:
    1/0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    logger.warning("Too many zeros floating around", exc_info=True)
```

body:
### Summary

The current spec for the `# ruff: ignore[rule]` format is flexible in terms of whitespaces and trailing commas. It would be nice to have a rule to enforce a unique format.

https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20line%20level%20suppression
```
The full inline comment specification is as follows:

    An inline blanket noqa comment is given by a case-insensitive match for #noqa with optional whitespace after the # symbol, followed by either: the end of the comment, the beginning of a new comment (#), or whitespace followed by any character other than :.
    An inline noqa suppression is given by first finding a case-insensitive match for #noqa with optional whitespace after the # symbol, optional whitespace after noqa, and followed by the symbol :. After this we are expected to have a list of rule codes which is given by sequences of uppercase ASCII characters followed by ASCII digits, separated by whitespace or commas. The list ends at the last valid code. We will attempt to interpret rules with a missing delimiter (e.g. F401F841), though a warning will be emitted in this case.
```

title: Formatter does not apply nested-string-quote-style alternation inside format-spec interpolations
body:
When the formatter normalizes an f-string's outer quotes to the configured `quote-style`, `nested-string-quote-style = "alternating"` (the default) is applied to string literals in normal interpolations, but not to string literals in interpolations **inside a format spec**.

```console
$ cat mini.py
a = f'x {d["k"]} y'
b = f'x {v:,.{d["n"]}f} y'
$ ruff format --isolated mini.py
1 file reformatted
$ cat mini.py
a = f"x {d['k']} y"
b = f"x {v:,.{d["n"]}f} y"
```

`a`: inner quotes alternated to `'`. `b`: the interpolation inside the format spec keeps `"`, reusing the outer quote.

```
invalid-syntax: Cannot reuse outer quote character in f-strings on Python 3.11 (syntax was added in Python 3.12)

label: linter
title: PLE0605 (invalid-all-format): consider flagging tuple `__all__`, not just non-sequence `__all__`
body:
### Summary

Currently `PLE0605` accepts either a `list` or a `tuple` for `__all__` and only flags other types:
```py
__all__ = ("Foo", "Bar")  # passes PLE0605 today
```
Guido, in [the PEP 844 discussion](https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-844-public-and-private-builtins/108515/113), states the intended contract more narrowly: `__all__` should specifically be a `list`, with anything else (including a `tuple`) treated as a deprecated-but-supported form:

> I propose to silently deprecate `__all__` that's not a list, supporting it forever, but documenting it as frowned upon. `@public` can issue a non-silent deprecation warning if it finds an existing `__all__` that isn't a list.

Request: update `PLE0605` to flag a tuple `__all__` as well, per this list-only contract.

One caveat worth resolving before implementing: `PLE0605` currently mirrors pylint's own `invalid-all-format` check, which also accepts `tuple`. Tightening ruff's version would diverge from pylint's behavior, so it may be it might be good to rename the rule while we're at it.

label: linter
title: Add rule checking for `if __name__ ==  "__main__":` clause in test files
body:
### Summary

```python
import pytest

def test_addition():
   assert 1 + 1 == 2

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pytest.main()
```
It is in my opinion much nicer to just have
```python
def test_addition():
   assert 1 + 1 == 2
```
and invoke the tests as (or whatever the file is called)
```pytest test_addition.py```

Even if you disagree with this, calling `pytest.main` does not raise a `SystemExit`, and only returns the return code (see documentation [here](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/usage.html#calling-pytest-from-python-code)). Thus the code in the first example I showed does not give an error (i.e. would pass in CI), even if the test fails.
A milder alternative could be to detect 
```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    pytest.main()
```
which should then be corrected to 
```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(pytest.main())
```
to properly fail if any of the tests fail.

label: linter
title: EXE rules differ from upstream
body:
While reviewing https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27037 and https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27702, especially the former, I realized that our EXE rules behave pretty differently from upstream overall. For example, this code produces two diagnostics in Ruff:

```py
hello = 1

hello #! not a shebang
```

[Playground](https://play.ruff.rs/34a8a71c-b8f2-4488-94eb-e8f7d69ed9ef)

and zero diagnostics with `flake8-executable`:

```console
❯ uvx --with flake8-executable flake8 example.py --select EXE
❯ echo $?
0
```

This is because flake8-executable stops looking for shebang lines at the first instance of Python code or the first shebang-like line, rather than checking all comments in the file like we do. I looked at the PRs adding these rules (https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/2118 and https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/2023), and while there are some tests demonstrating the divergent behavior, I didn't find any discussion that indicated it was really intentional. I also found that the fix introduced in https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/2183 for end-of-line "shebang" comments was regressed in https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/6039, so we even flag those now, as shown in the example above.

I think following the upstream behavior more closely would probably be an improvement and preferable over landing either of the narrower fixes in #27037 or #27702 on their own, but we should make that decision and apply it to all of the EXE rules at once, if desired.

label: linter
title: Detect dataclasses that silently override an inherited __hash__
body:
### Summary

Dataclasses may silently define or override `__hash__` if defined in a superclass. That produces gotcha's. Would be nice if there were a rule to catch this:

### Example

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass


class Base:
    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        return 42


@dataclass
class Child(Base):
    value: int
```

`Base` has a `__hash__` implementation, so it is reasonable to assume that `Child` inherits it.

However, `@dataclass` generates `__eq__` by default, and for `eq=True, frozen=False`, dataclasses set `__hash__ = None`. Consequently:

```python
hash(Base())    # works

hash(Child(1))  # TypeError: unhashable type: 'Child'
```

title: `ruff format --check` uses same exit code for syntax errors in files, and usage errors
body:
### Question

According to the documentation (https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/#exit-codes), `ruff format --check` has three exit codes:
* 0 if Ruff terminates successfully, and no files would be formatted if --check were not specified.
* 1 if Ruff terminates successfully, and one or more files would be formatted if --check were not specified.
* 2 if Ruff terminates abnormally due to invalid configuration, invalid CLI options, or an internal error.

Now if a file that `ruff format --check` looks at has a syntax error, `ruff format --check` also exits with exit code 2.

For me this is pretty bad, since I (as a CI tool that runs `ruff format --check`) cannot distinguish a usage error of ruff (bad parameters, invalid config, ...) from a perfectly valid thing that happens during regular use (namely syntax errors in files that should be formatted).

Would it be possible to add another exit code for errors in files that prevent ruff from formatting them, that is different from 2? Even using 1 for this would be a lot better than using 2.

### Version

0.16.1

label: linter
title: Avoid duplicate diagnostics from D400 and D415 when both rules are enabled
body:
## Summary

`D415` (`missing-terminal-punctuation`) is effectively a superset of `D400` (`missing-trailing-period`) for docstrings that do not end with any terminal punctuation.

When both rules are enabled, Ruff reports two diagnostics for the same underlying problem:

```python
def foo():
    """Return the value"""
```

Current output:

```
D400 First line should end with a period
D415 First line should end with a period, question mark, or exclamation point
```

This results in duplicate diagnostics for a single issue.

## Expected behavior

When both `D400` and `D415` are enabled, Ruff should emit only `D400` for docstrings that lack terminal punctuation entirely, since satisfying `D400` also satisfies `D415`.

## Alternative approach

**Another possible solution** would be to merge these two rules into a single rule with a configuration option controlling the allowed terminal punctuation.

For example:

* `period` (current `D400` behavior)
* `terminal-punctuation` (current `D415` behavior)

This would eliminate the overlap while preserving both styles as configurable options.

title: `strict-equality-semantics` and `replace-imports-with-any` should not be overridable at the file-level
body:
Is it okay and intentional that this setting can be overriden at a file level using override? Or should this be a setting that applies globally? If think it's probably fine, but we have to think about whether this changes inference results and could lead to inconsistent views between different files in the project.

I'm asking because `file_settings` currently merges all analysis settings.

_Originally posted by @MichaReiser in https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/26414#issuecomment-4933176939_
            
My review comment here was a bit vague, it wasn't explicit about when per-file-settings are okay. 

`strict-equality-semantics` changes how types are inferred, which in turn can change its public interface. Settings that change the inferred type must not be overridable at the file-level. Instead, those settings must be resolved and stored on `Program`. 

The reason why inference changing results can not be file-level is that the setting would only apply to the specific file, but not files its importing. The opposite also applies, files importing the file for which the setting is overridden now see the "overridden interface". Ultimately, this leads to inconsistent inference results within a `Program`, which we should avoid.

title: Rule idea: flag `ignore_zeros=True` in `tarfile` usage
body:
### Summary

From the [tarfile](https://docs.python.org/3/library/tarfile.html#tarfile.TarFile) docs:

> If ignore_zeros is [False](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#False), treat an empty block as the end of the archive. If it is [True](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#True), skip empty (and invalid) blocks and try to get as many members as possible. This is only useful for reading concatenated or damaged archives.

Setting this flag on `tarfile.open`, `tarfile.TarFile(...)`, or `tarfile.TarFile.open(...)` effectively puts Python's tar parser into a much more permissive mode than the default, one that is significantly more differential-prone. Most users _probably_ don't want this (and probably aren't even aware this flag exists).

label: linter
title: Ban `hmac/secrets.compare_digest()` on arbitrary strings
body:
### Summary

[`hmac.compare_digest()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hmac.html#hmac.compare_digest) (re-expored under `secrets`) accepts strings or byte-like objects. However, only ASCII strings are allowed. This is documented, but not as a warning which makes it quite hard to catch. While the Python docs could be improved, it would be valuable to have a Ruff rule imo.

Suggested rule: ban using the function if a non-literal string is used (or a non-ASCII literal), and recommend encoding it first:

```python
hmac.compare_digest("a", "a")  # fine, known ASCII string literals
hmac.compare_digest("é", "é")  # bad, non ASCII

# This probably requires type-aware analysis:
def compare(a: str, b: str):
    return hmac.compare_digest(a, b)  # bad, `a` and `b` are not guaranteed to be ASCII
```

label: configuration
title: DTZ rules should not be in the default set
body:
### Summary

In the latest version of `ruff`, [the `flake8-datetimez` rules](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/#flake8-datetimez-dtz) were added to the default rule set. As one of the maintainers of `datetime` in CPython and someone who has been writing about and giving talks about `datetime`s, I think this is *extremely* misguided.

I would keep `DTZ002` (don't use `datetime.datetime.today`), `DTZ003` and `DTZ004` ([don't use `utc(now|fromtimestamp)`](https://blog.ganssle.io/articles/2019/11/utcnow.html)), but that is it. DTZ901 (no `datetime.min`/`datetime.max` without a timezone) is probably the most bizarre one because it makes approximately zero sense to use a time zone with one of those: there are a bunch of weird edge cases when you do so, and they represent a time ~2000 years before time zones were invented and a time ~8000 years after the latest date where current time zone information is likely to be a good prediction of future offsets.

The main problem with all the other rules is that they fail to take into account that [naïve time zones are the only real way to represent system local time](https://blog.ganssle.io/articles/2022/04/naive-local-datetimes.html) in the `datetime` module. It is *extremely common* to want to work in the system local time zone. Having these rules on by default is going to teach people that you should do some very bad patterns like trying to guess what the system local time zone is, or picking a random time zone like "America/New_York" or something.

I strongly recommend making these rules opt-in.

title: `RUF038` changes runtime expressions and drops subscripted `Literal` members
body:
### Summary

RUF038 is documented as simplifying type annotations, but it also diagnoses runtime `Literal` expressions. Its traversal can additionally ignore a non-`Literal` subscript member and remove that member from the expression.

[Playground reproduction](https://play.ruff.rs/15202ceb-491e-4419-b430-3791511b065c)

```python
from typing import Literal, get_args


print(get_args(Literal[True, False]))

values = ["sentinel"]
print(get_args(Literal[True, False, values[0]]))
```

With unsafe fixes enabled, Ruff changes this to:

```python
from typing import get_args


print(get_args(bool))

values = ["sentinel"]
print(get_args(bool))
```

The output changes from `(True, False)` and `(True, False, 'sentinel')` to `()` and `()`. The second expression loses its third member and the evaluation of `values[0]`.

RUF038 should be limited to appropriate annotation contexts, and it should never collapse a `Literal` unless every member is known to be part of the supported replacement. This is distinct from #16129, which concerns type-checker compatibility for annotation fixes; these examples change runtime values and evaluation. This blocks #26919.

### Summary

The preview expansion of SIM113 treats some expressions as integer counters even though they do not evaluate to integers and cannot be used as an `enumerate` start value.

[Playground reproduction](https://play.ruff.rs/115c2af8-2c5a-4cab-b931-3be3c8788090)

```python
def print_items(items):
    index = 2**-1
    for item in items:
        print(index, item)
        index += 1


print_items(["a"])
```

Ruff reports SIM113 and suggests using `enumerate()`. The original code runs and prints `0.5 a`, but the corresponding rewrite:

```python
for index, item in enumerate(items, start=2**-1):
    print(index, item)
```

raises:

```console
TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
```

SIM113 should only diagnose inferred counter expressions that are guaranteed to be valid integer `enumerate` start values. This blocks #26946.

title: `RUF055` safe fix changes behavior for non-string inputs
body:
### Summary

The RUF055 fix is classified as safe, but it changes behavior when a bytes regular expression searches an object that implements the buffer protocol.

[Playground reproduction](https://play.ruff.rs/4b61dff1-5a7e-4e67-a671-42ef5d4a2f96)

```python
import re


assert re.search(b"ab", memoryview(b"abc"))
```

Ruff replaces the assertion with:

```python
assert b"ab" in memoryview(b"abc")
```

The original assertion passes. The replacement fails because `re.search` accepts the `memoryview` as a bytes-like search target, while membership on a `memoryview` does not perform a byte-subsequence search.

I think the rule probably should not apply unless we can confirm that the target is of the proper type, or at least we shouldn't offer a fix. This blocks #26908.

label: linter
title: `B006` preview fix changes multiline string literal contents
body:
### Summary

The preview fix for B006 changes the contents of multiline string literals when it moves a default expression into the function body.

[Playground reproduction](https://play.ruff.rs/e2b25e7c-6221-4c04-b9f9-171ab9cef8ec)

```python
def f(value=["""first
second"""]):
    return value


print(repr(f()))
```

Running:

```console
ruff check --preview --select B006 --unsafe-fixes --fix example.py
```

produces:

```python
def f(value=None):
    if value is None:
        value = ["""first
    second"""]
    return value
```

The original function returns `['first\nsecond']`; the fixed function returns `['first\n    second']`.

Without `--preview`, Ruff escapes the newline as `"""first\nsecond"""` and preserves the runtime value. This is therefore specific to the preview `b006_unsafe_fix_preserve_assignment_expr` behavior, not the longstanding `global`/`nonlocal` insertion-order bug.

The fix should preserve the exact runtime value of multiline literals. This blocks #26950 and, because #26952 is currently stacked on #26950, the stack as currently structured.

This part isn't strictly related, but the fix for B006 can also create a reference before a `global` or `nonlocal` statement: [Playground](https://play.ruff.rs/4c0635a6-a37f-439d-ab03-01ed42de2878)

title: `UP040` fix produces invalid syntax when a defaulted TypeVar precedes a non-defaulted TypeVar
body:
### Summary

The preview UP040 fix can emit an invalid PEP 695 type-parameter order when a defaulted `TypeVar` is followed by a non-defaulted `TypeVar`.

[Playground reproduction](https://play.ruff.rs/afd59d20-00a6-425d-983e-d8ce0e60cd28)

```python
from typing import TypeAlias, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T", default=int)
S = TypeVar("S")

Pair: TypeAlias = tuple[T, S]
```

With `--target-version py313 --preview --select UP040 --unsafe-fixes`, Ruff produces:

```python
type Pair[T = int, S] = tuple[T, S]
```

Ruff then rejects its own output:

```console
invalid-syntax: non default type parameter `S` follows default type parameter
```

UP040 should not offer a fix in this case unless it can generate a valid and equivalent type-parameter list. This blocks #26948.

This also affects UP046 and UP047.

label: linter
title: [`ruff`] Extend RUF059 to flag unpackings where every target is unused
body:
## Summary

When **all** targets of an unpacking assignment are unused, `RUF059`'s per-variable fix produces bindings that are pointless as a whole:

```python
_a, _b = f()          # after RUF059 fix — nothing is ever read
```

Here the assignment conveys nothing. If the call matters only for its side effects, it shouldn't bind a tuple at all:

```python
f()
```

I'd like `RUF059` to detect the "every target unused" case and suggest dropping the assignment.

## Behavior

Trigger when an unpacking has no subsequently-used target:

- `a, b = f()` — neither used
- `_a, _b = f()` — the post-RUF059-fix shape
- `_, _ = f()` — all dummies (currently invisible to RUF059, since every target matches `dummy-variable-rgx`)

Do **not** trigger when at least one target is used (`a, _b = f()` stays as-is).

## Fix

Strip the target list, keep the RHS as an expression statement — safe because side effects are preserved:

```diff
- _a, _b = f()
+ f()
```

Removing the whole line (dead when the RHS is pure) could be an unsafe fix, since purity generally isn't known.

The fix for [`write-whole-file` (FURB103)](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/write-whole-file/) can change the program’s behavior. `open` truncates the file. If the `write` call fails because the argument is of the wrong type, nothing is written, but the file is still already truncated. The fixed version checks the type before opening the file, so if the type is wrong, the file is not truncated.         f.write(b"\103")
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)
contents = pathlib.Path("furb103.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print(f"{contents=}")
# EOF

write() argument must be str, not bytes

title: [`flake8-async`] Allow configuring safe decorators for `ASYNC119`
body:
### Summary

`ASYNC119` uses a hard-coded allowlist of decorators that guarantee async-generator cleanup, including `contextlib.asynccontextmanager`, pytest fixtures, and `trio.as_safe_channel`.

Other frameworks can provide the same lifecycle guarantee. Dishka, for example, finalizes generator-based providers when their scope exits.

The following complete example runs successfully but triggers `ASYNC119`:

```python
import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass

from dishka import Provider, Scope, make_async_container, provide


@dataclass
class Resource:
    closed: bool = False


@asynccontextmanager
async def open_resource() -> AsyncIterator[Resource]:
    resource = Resource()
    try:
        yield resource
    finally:
        resource.closed = True


class MyProvider(Provider):
    @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    async def resource(self) -> AsyncIterator[Resource]:
        async with open_resource() as resource:
            yield resource  # ASYNC119


async def main() -> None:
    root = make_async_container(MyProvider())

    async with root() as request_container:
        resource = await request_container.get(Resource)
        assert resource.closed is False

    assert resource.closed is True
    await root.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

Reproduced with Ruff 0.15.21 and Dishka 1.10.1:

```console
$ ruff check --preview --select ASYNC119 example.py
ASYNC119 Yield in context manager in async generator may not trigger cleanup

$ python example.py
# exits successfully
```

Adding `@asynccontextmanager` is not an equivalent workaround because it changes the callable's runtime interface and is incompatible with Dishka's generator-provider handling.

### Proposed solution

Allow users to configure additional safe decorators:

```toml
[tool.ruff.lint.flake8-async]
safe-async-generator-decorators = ["dishka.provide"]
```

label: configuration
title: Improve support for arbitrary functions accepting `TypeForm` arguments
body:
With the acceptance and implementation of PEP 747 in mypy and being no longer locked behind a feature-flag as of mypy 2.2 we can expect usage of `TypeForm` to increase, which includes functions that don't necessarily use the argument at runtime like `typing.cast`.

As a result there will be custom functions like that accept stringified forward references that ruff will not treat as forward references, so we will see false positives for rules like F401 and TC001-004.

Similar to the `extend-generics` setting, we may want to add something like a `extend-type-form-callables` setting which accepts a mapping of function names, to a list of argument names/positions, so we can treat the relevant subexpressions as typing expressions.

E.g. for `typing.cast` the configuration could look like this:

```toml
[lint.extend-type-form-callables]
"typing.cast" = [0, "typ"]
```

Meaning the first argument positionally and the `typ` keyword argument will be interpreted as a type expression on any call that resolves to the configured callable name, i.e. in this case `typing.cast`.

Eventually we could automate this with multi-file analysis by inspecting the parameter annotations of the called function, but for now a custom setting should be good enough.

label: configuration
title: `ruff check --add-noqa` / `--fix` / `ruff format` truncate source files to 0 bytes on SIGINT (non-atomic in-place write)
body:
## Summary

`ruff check --add-noqa` (and presumably `--fix` / `ruff format`) rewrites
source files in place without an atomic-rename step. If the process is
interrupted (SIGINT / crash) while a write is in flight, the affected files
are left truncated to 0 bytes — neither the old content nor the new content
survives.

The cache path was hardened against this in #9981 ("Use atomic write when
persisting cache"). The same pattern hasn't been applied to source-file
writes.

## Repro

1. Run `ruff check --add-noqa` (or `ruff format`, or `ruff check --fix`)
   against a large tree where many files will be rewritten.
2. SIGINT (Ctrl-C) it mid-run, while ruff is rewriting files in parallel.
3. `find <tree> -name '*.py' -empty` — a handful of files that previously
   had content are now 0 bytes. Their mtimes cluster tightly around the
   SIGINT.

## Expected

An interrupted in-place rewrite should leave the original file intact (or
the fully-written new file), never an empty / partially-written file.
Standard pattern: write to `<file>.tmp`, `fsync`, then `rename` over the
original — `rename(2)` is atomic on POSIX, so a crash anywhere before the
rename leaves the original untouched.

## Prior art in-repo

#9981 introduced atomic-rename for cache writes for exactly this reason.
The same fix shape (write-tmp + rename) should apply to the source-write
path used by `--add-noqa`, `--fix`, and `ruff format`.

## Version

ruff 0.14.10, Linux (Docker, ext4).

label: configuration
title: `exclude` is resolved relative to cwd, not config dir, with `--config`
body:
### Summary

## Summary

With an explicit `--config <path>`, `exclude` / `extend-exclude` patterns are
matched against the target path **relative to the current working directory**,
not relative to the configuration file's directory. So the same config excludes
a directory when ruff runs from the project root, but **formats files inside
that excluded directory** when ruff runs from a subdirectory. A leading `**/`
does not help — the parent path components are absent from the cwd-relative path.

This breaks editors and build tools that invoke ruff from a subdirectory with an
explicit config.

This is the same root cause as #12058, but for `exclude`/`extend-exclude` rather
than `per-file-ignores`.

## Reproduction

```bash
docker run --rm alchemmist/ruff-exclude-repro
```

It builds the tree, prints the config and the exact commands, and shows ruff's
own diff output proving the leak, for ruff 0.14.1 and 0.15.19.

<details>
<summary>Manual reproduction & full details</summary>

`ruff.toml` at the project root:

```toml
force-exclude = true
extend-exclude = ["**/libra/tests/py2_legacy/**"]
```

Tree (both files badly formatted, so `ruff format` wants to rewrite them):

```
user_sessions/
  ruff.toml
  libra/src/good.py                  # normal, should be formatted
  libra/tests/py2_legacy/legacy.py   # python2 legacy, should be EXCLUDED
```

```console
# from the project root — correct: only good.py is touched
$ cd user_sessions && ruff format . --config ruff.toml --diff
--- libra/src/good.py
1 file would be reformatted

# from a subdirectory — WRONG: the excluded file is reformatted too
$ cd user_sessions/libra && ruff format . --config ../ruff.toml --diff
--- src/good.py
--- tests/py2_legacy/legacy.py    # <-- excluded file leaks
2 files would be reformatted
```

**Expected:** the excluded directory is excluded regardless of cwd — ideally
`exclude`/`extend-exclude` anchored to the config file's directory.

**Actual:** the exclude is anchored to the cwd; from a subdir

It found a few, roughly in order of decreasing severity: ## 1. Shared autofixes can modify imports protected by `ruff:ignore` Given: ```py from package import ( kept, # noqa: F401 removed, ) from package2 import ( kept2, # ruff:ignore[F401] removed2, ) ``` [Playground](https://play.ruff.rs/b1b2fda5-1fef-462b-9f19-d0d7863e32d8) With `noqa`, `kept` is preserved, while `ruff:ignore` suppresses the diagnostic but allows the fix for `removed2` to remove the whole import.

This happens because `Checker::rule_is_ignored` only checks `noqa` directives. It is used while constructing shared import fixes so that suppressed imports can be excluded before the fix is generated. The affected rules appear to be: - `F401` - `TC001` - `TC002` - `TC003` - `TC004`

label: server
title: [LSP] Working directory should not affect functionality
body:
### Summary

A user of `LSP-ruff` (Sublime Text package integrating ruff) [reported an issue](https://github.com/sublimelsp/LSP/pull/2966) about ruff/ty behaving differently depending on which working directory is being set when starting the server.

In the LSP world the working directory should in theory not matter or affect functionality since this is not really relevant there and the LSP spec doesn't specify anything related to that. The closest relevant thing is probably [WorkspaceFolders](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.18/specification/#workspaceFolder) sent during initialization but in this particular case (when opening individual files), those are not set.

The user's report says:

> If open file (eg. double click in file explorer or Open file from ST menu) - servers starts in installation dir of ST:
LSP: starting ['C:\\Users\\...\\LSP-ty\\v0.0.50\\ty.exe', 'server'] in C:\Program Files\Sublime Text
The server is expected to run in the directory of the file being edited for full functionality.
If the server is started in the wrong directory, not all functions will work (eg. rename or completeFunctionParentheses).

I'm thinking that, in LSP mode, it's the server's responsibility to figure out the best "working directory" for a given file. If no workspace folders are provided then maybe it should infer it from the open file. But note that the user might open another file from a completely different location next...

If that is not feasible, maybe server could introduce some custom logic for handling files outside workspace folder. I think rust-analyzer does something similar where it [passes opened files through a dedicated initialization option](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/69ccffdb5b3570c6c14c5780bf2e8836f2209d90/editors/code/src/ctx.ts#L243-L247). Not a big fan of that solution but if there is no other option...

### Version

ruff 0.15.17

label: linter
title: Numpy rule request: prohibit use of bool(my_numpy_array)
body:
### Summary

Many times, I've encountered runtime errors trying to do something like:

```py
if my_numpy_array:
```

My expectation is often that this conditional would evaluate to False if `my_numpy_array` is None or is empty, which is the exact behavior I get from lists. But in reality I get a `ValueError` exception at runtime:

```
ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all()
```

While I'd love if numpy would change their `__bool__` implementation to match that of `list`, I'd be almost as happy if ruff (or I suppose ty) could statically catch cases where I try to check the condition of a numpy array, so that I don't have to wait until runtime to discover I messed up.

title: Formatter: Vertical alignment for tabular-like literals
body:
This is another request for preserving vertical alignment in the formatter (see also: #24611 and #7684)

Automatic formatting should improve readability, but for table-like data literals, removing intentional intra-line spacing can make code significantly harder to read. This affects common patterns such as numeric matrices, sparse arrays, parameter grids, tabular test cases, and dictionaries whose values are homogeneous records.

In these cases, vertical alignment is not merely cosmetic: it communicates the tabular structure and allows values to be compared column-wise. Without it, logical columns disappear visually, and a single long entry can make the table shape hard to recognize.

The current workaround is `# fmt: skip` or `# fmt: off`, followed by manual formatting. That works, but disables formatting more broadly than necessary. If detecting such cases heuristically is too difficult or controversial, would an explicit opt-in pragma be viable? For example:

```python
EXPERIMENTS = {
    # model                                                   lr      batch  dropout  seed
    "mlp":                                                    (1e-3,   256,   0.00,     0),
    "resnet18":                                               (3e-4,   128,   0.10,     1),
    "vit_b16":                                                (1e-4,    64,   0.00,     2),
    "efficientnetv2_xl_imagenet21k_ft1k":                     (3e-5,    32,   0.20,     3),
    "swin_transformer_large_patch4_window12_384_in22k":       (1e-5,     8,   0.10,     4),
    "experimental_multimodal_foundation_encoder_v2026_06_06": (5e-6,     4,   0.30,     5),
}  # fmt: tabular
```

Unlike `# fmt: skip`, this would not disable formatting entirely, but would preserve or apply vertical alignment for selected tabular literals.

Let's look at some examples which clearly demonstrate the degratation in readability due to the formatter: [[playground]](https://play.ruff.rs/403edfe5-f203-47dd-9208-ba3b6e80b9a8)

title: [NPY201] np.in1d cannot be cleanly replaced with np.isin
body:
### Summary

The current NPY201 rule replaces `np.in1d` with a call to `np.isin`. However, this is not a true drop in replacement, as for non-1d inputs, `np.isin` reuses the input shape. For example

```
>>> np.in1d(np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]), [2, 3, 5, 7])
array([False,  True,  True, False,  True, False])

>>> np.isin(np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]), [2, 3, 5, 7])
array([[False,  True,  True],
       [False,  True, False]])
```

As is, running `ruff check --select NPY201 --fix` can introduce new bugs because of this. I think that a more correct replacement would be to replace `np.in1d(x)` with `np.isin(x).ravel()`.

label: server
title: ruff server: codeAction/resolve with missing or malformed data crashes the server
body:
## Summary

`ruff server` assumes that every `codeAction/resolve` request contains a valid document URI in `CodeAction.data`.

If `data` is missing, `null`, not a URL string, or an invalid URL string, the server panics while preparing the background task and exits instead of returning `InvalidParams`.

I reproduced this on current `main` after a normal `initialize` request by sending:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "method": "codeAction/resolve",
  "params": {
    "title": "Ruff: Fix all auto-fixable problems",
    "kind": "source.fixAll.ruff"
  }
}
```

These variants also crash:
- `"data": null`
- `"data": {"uri": "file:///tmp/x.py"}`
- `"data": "not-a-url"`

Observed result:
- `ruff server` exits with status `101`
- stderr shows a panic from `crates/ruff_server/src/server/api/requests/code_action_resolve.rs`

The root cause appears to be:
- `CodeActionResolve::document_url` deserializes `params.data.clone().unwrap_or_default()` and calls `expect(...)`
- this happens during background task setup in `background_request_task`, before the request-level `catch_unwind`
- the panic then propagates out of the main loop thread and exits the server

Expected result:
Malformed `codeAction/resolve` input should return `InvalidParams` instead of panicking or exiting the server.

One additional note: `ruff server` advertises `codeActionProvider.resolveProvider = true` unconditionally. I have not confirmed that a mainstream editor hits this path on its own, but a malformed `codeAction/resolve` request currently crashes the server.

## Version

`ruff 0.15.14`

Source checkout: `0909c7ec2159` (`main` on 2026-05-23)

label: formatter
title: Markdown formatter mishandles closing code fences
body:
## Summary

The Markdown formatter treats closing code fences too strictly in one direction and too loosely in another.

In `crates/ruff_markdown/src/lib.rs`, the same code fence regex is used for both opening and closing fences, and the formatter currently requires the closing fence string to be exactly equal to the opening fence string.

That creates two visible formatting issues:

- A valid closing fence that is longer than the opening fence is missed, so the Python block is treated as unclosed and is not formatted.
- A line with non-whitespace info after the fence can be treated as a closing fence, so Ruff can format only part of the intended fenced block.

## Reproduction

A longer closing fence should close this block:

~~~markdown
```py
print( 'hello' )
````
~~~

Expected formatted output:

~~~markdown
```py
print("hello")
````
~~~

A fence with trailing non-whitespace content should not close this block:

~~~markdown
```py
print( 'hello' )
```not_a_close
print( 'world' )
```
~~~

Expected behavior: ` ```not_a_close` is treated as code content, not as the closing fence.

## Cause

Closing fence detection should match the Markdown rule used elsewhere in the formatter: the fence character must match, the closing fence must be at least as long as the opening fence, and any trailing content after the fence must be whitespace only.

label: linter
title: Add an opt-in rule to prefer `from x import y` over `import x`
body:
## Summary

It would be useful to have an opt-in lint rule that enforces a preference for explicit `from x import y` imports when imported module members are used directly in the file, instead of keeping a broader `import x` and accessing members as `x.y`.

## Motivation

Some projects prefer imports that make dependencies visible at the import site and keep call sites concise. For example:

```python
import pathlib

path = pathlib.Path("example.txt")
```

could be reported as:

```python
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("example.txt")
```

This style can improve readability in codebases where qualified module access adds noise, especially for frequently used classes, functions, or constants. It also makes the specific imported API surface clearer during review.

Ruff already has related import-style functionality, such as `manual-from-import` (`PLR0402`), but that rule only covers a narrower pattern involving aliased submodule imports. A more general, explicitly opt-in rule would allow teams with this convention to enforce it consistently without affecting Ruff users who prefer qualified imports.

## Proposed behavior

Add a disabled-by-default rule that detects cases where:

```python
import module

module.name(...)
```

can be rewritten as:

```python
from module import name

name(...)
```

The rule should be conservative and avoid unsafe rewrites, for example when the module object itself is used, when name collisions would be introduced, or when the rewrite would make the code less clear.

## Why opt-in

Both styles are valid and commonly used. Some projects intentionally prefer qualified imports because they make the origin of a symbol visible at every call site. For that reason, this rule should not be part of any default rule set, but it would be valuable for projects that deliberately choose the opposite convention.

Thanks for considering this enhancement.

title: Rule idea: class-level None can make runtime protocol checks slow
body:
# Rule idea: class-level `None` can make runtime protocol checks slow

Ruff could flag statically-obvious cases where a structural implementation of a large `@runtime_checkable Protocol` stores a protocol member as literal class-level `None`.

CPython treats this as satisfying non-callable protocol attributes, but it prevents the fast ABC cache path from warming.
Repeated `isinstance(obj, ProtocolType)` checks can then scale with the protocol member count.
Related CPython issue: <https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/102433>.

Small benchmark on Python 3.14.4:

```python
from timeit import timeit
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

MEMBERS = 100
LOOPS = 200_000

P = runtime_checkable(type("P", (Protocol,), {
    "__annotations__": {f"a{i}": object for i in range(MEMBERS)},
}))

Fast = type("Fast", (), {f"a{i}": True for i in range(MEMBERS)})
Slow = type("Slow", (), {
    **{f"a{i}": True for i in range(MEMBERS - 1)},
    f"a{MEMBERS - 1}": None,
})

fast = Fast()
slow = Slow()

label: linter
title: D1XX for private code
body:
### Summary

Currently, the rules D1XX (AKA D1*, D1**) only detect missing documentation in public code (= functions, methods, modules, classes, etc.). For example, D103 only detects missing documentation of public functions, not of private functions (e.g., those whose names start with `_`).

I'd like to force myself to write documentation for all functions (save for the usual exceptions such as `@overload`, `@override`, etc.), even private ones. The reasons to do so are as follows:

- Documentation is not only written for library users, or end users of a program, but also for all developers of a package, including oneself (who still knows after a year what a complex function is doing?). Also, I often look into the source code of upstream packages for debugging, creating issues, etc. Having documentation obviously makes it easier to understand code for these user groups.
- I regularly make previously private functions/methods public when I decide that other classes, modules, or even downstream users should be able to use them. With the current D1XX rules, you have to write documentation in this case (remember, the function might be pretty old) if the function didn't have any. If you enforce documentation on all code, going back and forth between public and private functions is much easier.

The solution I'd propose is either

- (preferred) to add an option that allows applying the existing D1XX rules to private code as well, with the option being set to “public only” by default to be backward-compatible, or
- to clone the D1* rules, make the cloned rules applicable to private code only (not public code), and disable the cloned rules by default.

To implement the first option, this check would need to be disabled if the option is set to “private and public code”:

https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/b81d55ed7006089dcbea80a135b6b8a91c1ed1fd/crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/pydocstyle/rules/not_missing.rs#L574-L576

title: New rule: `cast()` should always be a standalone assignment
body:
### Summary

Add a lint rule that flags any `cast()` call that is not the sole right-hand side of a simple assignment statement.

**Motivation**
`cast()` is a type-system-only annotation with no runtime effect. When combined with other expressions, it obscures both the computation and the type assertion:

```py
# Bad
x = cast(MyType, some_function(arg1, arg2))
return cast("dict[str, Any]", json.loads(json.dumps(kwargs)))

# Good
x = some_function(arg1, arg2)
x = cast(MyType, x)

json_kwargs = json.loads(json.dumps(kwargs))
return cast("dict[str, Any]", json_kwargs)
```


---

It could also be argued that, e.g., `return cast(MyType, x)` should be flagged as the goal is to split functionality from typing information.

title: Additional false positives in `PLR1733` and `PLR1736`
body:
This is a follow-up issue to https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/25150, tracking a couple of additional false positives. https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/25177 fixed the first one:

```py
def foo(d: dict):
    for k, v in d.items():
        ...
    else:
        print(d[k])  # resolved false positive
```

This was a false positive because `k` may be unbound in the `else` clause if the loop is never entered:

```pycon
>>> for k, v in {}.items():
...     ...
... else:
...     print(k)
...
Traceback (most recent call last):
File "<python-input-0>", line 4, in <module>
  print(k)
        ^
NameError: name 'k' is not defined
```

This also applies to [unnecessary-list-index-lookup (PLR1736)](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unnecessary-list-index-lookup/#unnecessary-list-index-lookup-plr1736):

```pycon
>>> for k, v in enumerate([]):
...     ...
... else:
...     print(k)
...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-1>", line 4, in <module>
    print(k)
          ^
NameError: name 'k' is not defined
```

Although we currently flag this too: https://play.ruff.rs/da8e5ff1-0dba-4e59-a5c1-a84428e92819

The other class of issue I noticed was that we also emit diagnostics if the key or value variable is shadowed:

```py
def foo(d: dict):
    for k, v in d.items():
        for k in foo:
            print(d[k])  # not the same `k` as the `.items()` loop
        for v in foo:
            print(d[k])  # not the same `v` as the `.items()` loop
```

This only seems to be the case if the shadowing binding comes from a `for` loop, so I suspect we're checking the `BindingKind` but not the actual location of the binding. We should fix these too.

## Summary
- [ ] Fix `else` handling in `PLR1736`
- [ ] Fix shadowing in `PLR1733`
- [ ] Fix shadowing in `PLR1736`

title: `requires-python` discovery is inconsistent with config file discovery
body:
### Summary

Hello, I've bumped into an issue related to #24829 and #14813.

The fix in #16319 improved `requires-python` inference, and the current behaviour conforms to [rule 3 of "Inferring the Python version"](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/configuration/#inferring-the-python-version). However, there's a UX gap: the inference only works when ruff's **cwd** is inside the project. When ruff is invoked from outside the project (passing the file by path), the user-level `target-version` wins over the project's `requires-python` — because rule 3 searches ancestors of the **cwd**, not ancestors of the file.

This is surprising because config file discovery walks up from the **file being linted**, while `requires-python` inference walks up from the **cwd**. These use different starting points for the same file. This is particularly relevant for those projects which don't configure ruff themselves in their own `pyproject.toml`, as well as editor integrations (e.g. VS Code) where the workspace root may be a parent directory of the project.

## Reproduction

Ruff version: 0.15.6

**1. Project setup** (`~/ruff_test/pyproject.toml`):

```toml
[project]
name = "ruff-target-test"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
```

Note: no `[tool.ruff]` section, i.e. not discovered as a "config".

```python

# UP042: StrEnum suggestion — only valid on py311+
class Foo(str, Enum):
    BAR = "bar"


# UP047: PEP 695 type params — only valid on py312+

def identity(x: T) -> T:

**3. User-level config** (`~/.config/ruff/ruff.toml`):

```toml

```bash

$ cd ~/ruff_test && ruff check --select UP042,UP047 test.py

$ ruff check --show-settings test.py 2>&1 | grep unresolved_target
linter.unresolved_target_version = 3.10

# Proposal: `WidePolymorphicReturn`

## Help Text

`[WidePolymorphicReturn] - Consider overloading this function to narrow the return type.`

## When to Trigger Rule

This lint rule will trigger against a **function definition** when the following two conditions are met:

1. At least one of the function’s arguments is the union of multiple types (type definition contains `typing.Union` or the pipe operator `|`)
2. The return type is the union of multiple types (type definition contains `typing.Union` or the pipe operator `|`)

## Details

When a function’s return type depends on one or more of its arguments’ types, it is preferable to `@overload` the function to tighter function signatures. Not doing this leaves the return type definition too wide—placing undue burden on the caller to narrow a type that could have been determined statically. 

Consider this (admittedly contrived) example:

```python
def identity(arg: str | int): -> str | int:
    return arg
```

```python
from . import identity

reveal_type(identity(“s”))  # int | str
reveal_type(identity(1))  # int | str
```

The solution is to provide overloads for each case: `int` or `str`. 

```python
from typing import overload 

@overload
def identity(arg: str) -> str: ...
@overload
def identity(arg: int) -> int: ...
def identity(arg: str | int): -> str | int:
    return arg
```

Doing this will provide the caller with narrower, more accurate type information. 

```python

reveal_type(identity(“s”))  # str
reveal_type(identity(1))  # int
```

### Summary

With the new PEP-810 lazy imports in Python 3.15, it's possible to write code like this:

```python
lazy import foo

class Bar(foo.Foo): ...
```

where the "lazy" import gets resolved immediately at module load time. That isn't what the user intended, so linters should warn against it.

The rule should check for names created through a lazy import and used either in the module global scope (and not within an except block or conditional block) or in a class body that is immediately within the global scope. More ambitiously, we could also check function bodies that we detect are called directly from the module scope (e.g. decorators, dataclass annotations). Doing this in full generality is obviously intractable, but some heuristics could go a long way.

I'm not sure the rule should have an autofix. Removing "lazy" is an obvious solution, but it may not be what the user wants: if they wrote `lazy` they probably intended it to be lazy, and we should give them a chance to fix their code.

label: linter
title: Add NPY rule: prefer np.allclose(a, b) over np.all(np.isclose(a, b))
body:
### Summary

It would be useful to have a rule under the `NPY` category that flags `np.all(np.isclose(...))` and suggests `np.allclose(...)` as a fix.

### Motivation

`np.allclose(a, b)` is a direct shorthand for `np.all(np.isclose(a, b))` — it's documented as such in the [NumPy reference](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.allclose.html), returns a Python `bool` instead of a 0-d array, and is more idiomatic. The two forms accept the same `rtol`/`atol`/`equal_nan` parameters, so the rewrite is mechanical and safe.

This pattern shows up frequently in test suites (e.g. `assert np.all(np.isclose(x, y))`) where authors reach for `isclose` first and wrap it in `all` rather than recalling that `allclose` exists.

### Example

```python
# Bad
assert np.all(np.isclose(values, expected))
assert np.all(np.isclose(values, expected, rtol=1e-5))

# Good
assert np.allclose(values, expected)
assert np.allclose(values, expected, rtol=1e-5)
```

label: linter
title: Add rules to check for dependencies missing a minimum version in `pyproject.toml`
body:
## Suggestion

Add rules to check that:

 - Each **required dependency** has a minimum allowed version
 - Each **optional dependency** has a minimum allowed version
 - Each **dependency group dependency** has a minimum allowed version 

## Motivation

Specifying the minimum allowed version of dependencies is a really helpful practice, though it's somewhat common for packages to not specify the minimum versions of its dependencies (for example, in the scientific pythoniverse).

The ``lowest`` and ``lowest-direct`` resolution strategies of uv solve for an environment with the lowest allowed versions of _all_ dependencies and _direct_ dependencies, respectively.

I've found the ``lowest`` resolution strategy to be fraught with peril since, in practice, it requires that all indirect dependencies list a minimum allowed version for each of their dependencies. If not, then some packages will be installed with their first release on PyPI (like `v0.0.0.1` 😅) which often is missing critical features.  

## Alternative possibilities

It would be great to have an autofix, though I'd propose including it in uv (e.g., https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/7515) since it would likely require querying PyPI.

## Gratitude

Thank you to everyone for creating a wonderful package!

Expressions would go directly from single-line (Layout 1) to one-per-line with trailing comma (Layout 3).

If adopted as the default, this also resolves the long-standing [`COM812`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/missing-trailing-comma/) formatter incompatibility (#9216).

The formatter produces three layouts for comma-separated content:

### Summary

The automatic fix for [PTH110](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/os-path-exists/#os-path-exists-pth110) changes runtime behaviour if path existence is checked against an empty string: `os.path.exists("")` always returns `False`, while `pathlib.Path("").exists()` always returns `True` (this is a deliberate choice on pathlib's side, see [here](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/112484#issuecomment-1863467295)).

label: linter
title: Allow first argument of class methods in metaclasses to be called `mcls`
body:
### Summary

`N804` currently triggers whenever the first argument of a method bound to a class is not called `cls`, as that violates PEP 8 naming conventions. However, `mcls` as an argument name is acceptable and in fact adopted in python. It is in some sense an implicit convention, primarily to avoid confusion (the first argument of instance methods of metaclasses, in particular `__subclasscheck__` and `__instancecheck__`, is usually called `cls`, and the analogous rule `N805` does not trigger in these cases). It occurs three times in the python docs, and in the python source as well. See [the annotationlib page](https://docs.python.org/3/library/annotationlib.html#recipes), [this howto](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/descriptor.html#member-objects-and-slots) and [the abc module source](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/8fc66aef6d7b3ae58f43f5c66f9366cc8cbbfcd2/Lib/abc.py#L105) for examples).

I propose to silence `N804` in these cases. Specifically, when the wrapped function of an instance of `classmethod`, a `__new__` method, an `__init_subclass__` method or a `__class_getitem__` method in the body of a subclass of `type` names its first argument `mcls`, the rule should be special-cased not to raise. For one, the VS Code Pylance extension, even in strict mode, does not complain about my usage of `mcls`.

body:
### Summary

I discovered today that ruff's PTH rules include a rule to suggest that `open(path)` be replaced with `path.open()`.

I tell my students that they should make the opposite change: replace all `path.open()` uses with `open(path)`.

My reasoning is that:

1. `pathlib.Path.open` was created because the built-in `open` function did not yet accept `pathlib.Path` objects
2. When Python 3.6 was released, the `open` function gained support for accepting `pathlib.Path` objects
3. The fact that `open` now accepts `pathlib.Path` objects means that `pathlib.Path.open` is no longer necessary

I consider `pathlib.Path.open` a relic from Python 3.4/3.5 (I called it such [in this talk](https://youtu.be/7XuyYDde-0A?si=HRNAH2nXSv1zT2Z4&t=1203)). I suspect I am not alone in this view, but I also assume some may dispute it (especially given that rules like PTH123 exist).

I would appreciate a rule that looks for `pathlib.Path.open` uses and recommends using the built-in `open` function instead. I would also like to hear what others think about my recommendation in that direction. Am I wrong, and if so, why?

By the way, I appreciate your links to my 2 blog posts from 2018/2019 advocating the wider adoption of pathlib. In [one of them](https://treyhunner.com/2018/12/why-you-should-be-using-pathlib/#pathlib_makes_the_simple_cases_simpler) I actually hinted the Python 3.6 `pathlib.Path.open` to `open` migration (but Python 3.4 and 3.5 hadn't reached their EOL at that time so I didn't recommend it as the sole approach).

Realizing that this may also warrant a discussion from the wider Python community, I've also opened [a discuss.python.org post on this topic](https://discuss.python.org/t/recommend-against-or-for-pathlib-path-open/106904).

PEP 723 inline script metadata is widely adopted (`uv`, `hatch`, `pdm`, `pipx`, `pip 26+`), but ruff's existing `pyproject.toml` validation (RUF200) doesn't apply to these blocks. Since `# /// script` blocks are embedded in comments, typos and structural errors go unnoticed until runtime.

This issue tracks **extending existing `pyproject.toml` lint rules to PEP 723 inline script blocks**. New lint rules that don't exist for `pyproject.toml` yet are tracked in astral-sh/ty#4264.

### 1. Invalid TOML in metadata block (error)

### Summary

Hey!

A common gotcha when using [`PermissionRequiredMixin`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.1/topics/auth/default/#the-permissionrequiredmixin-mixin) in django class based view is to place it last in your subclass hierarchy for ex:

```python
class MyView(View, PermissionRequiredMixin):
    permission_required = "polls.add_choice"


```

Doing so, it actually **never checks the permissions** because of the MRO. The `dispatch` method from the `View` class will be called and because it doesn't call `super()`, `PermissionRequiredMixin.dispatch` is silently skipped.

This can very easily lead to security concerns.

Would it make sense to add a rule to the `flake8-django` ruleset swapping the base classes automatically if the `PermissionRequiredMixin` is not the first base class ?

body:
### Summary

[for-loop-writes (FURB122)](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/for-loop-writes/#for-loop-writes-furb122) says 
> When writing a batch of elements, it's more idiomatic to use a single method call to IOBase.writelines, rather than write elements one by one.

That rule checks for `write` in loop, but sequential `write` calls, which match the exact same reasoning, are not flagged.

Given the following example, should either cases be caught?

```py
import pathlib

# from
def foo(fname: str) -> None:
    with pathlib.Path(fname).open("w", encoding="utf-8") as output:
        output.write("a\n")
        output.write("b\n")
        output.write("c\n")
        for subtitle, suffix in (
            ("Overviews", "_overview"),
            ("Modules", "_modules"),
            ("Objects", "_objects"),
        ):
            output.write(f"{suffix} {subtitle}\n")
        output.write("d\n")

# to
def foo(fname: str) -> None:
    with pathlib.Path(fname).open("w", encoding="utf-8") as output:
        output.writelines(("a\n", "b\n", "c\n"))
        output.writelines(
            f"{suffix} {subtitle}\n"
            for subtitle, suffix in (
                ("Overviews", "_overview"),
                ("Modules", "_modules"),
                ("Objects", "_objects"),
            )
        )
        output.write("d\n")

# or even, if we take collection-literal-concatenation (RUF005) into account
def foo(fname: str) -> None:
    with pathlib.Path(fname).open("w", encoding="utf-8") as output:
        output.writelines(
            [
                "a\n",
                "b\n",
                "c\n",
                *[
                    f"{suffix} {subtitle}\n"
                    for subtitle, suffix in (
                        ("Overviews", "_overview"),
                        ("Modules", "_modules"),
                        ("Objects", "_objects"),
                    )
                ],
                "d\n",

        )

title: Stop inserting a trailing comma on the final parameter
body:
### Summary

Currently, when Ruff formats parameters into separate lines due to exceeding the maximum line length, it automatically appends a trailing comma to the final parameter. This behavior prevents the formater from collapsing those parameters back onto a single line, even after subsequent code changes reduce the line length below the threshold.

While the `skip-magic-trailing-comma = true` setting addresses this specific shrinking issue, it introduces a new limitation: it removes the ability for users to manually keep parameters on separate lines when the line length is not exceeded, which is valued for maintaining code readability and anticipating future growth as [illustrated in the Black documentation](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/current_style.html#the-magic-trailing-comma:~:text=However%2C%20there%20are%20cases%20where%20you%20put%20a%20short%20collection%20or%20function%20call%20in%20your%20code%20but%20you%20anticipate%20it%20will%20grow%20in%20the%20future.).

I suggest that Ruff should not append a trailing comma to the final parameter when it formats parameters into separate lines. The presence of a trailing comma should be treated solely as a user-driven instrument.

```python
f"{banana}" % banana
f"hello %s %s" % (1, 2)
```

produces no warnings, even though mixing f-string interpolation with `%`-formatting is almost certainly a mistake — both serve the same purpose.

## Proposal

Add a new rule (RUF072) that flags any use of `%` on an f-string. I can't think of a valid use case where using `%` over f-string interpolation is desired.

## Related

- #24031 — original report
- #24142 — F507 fix for non-tuple RHS

title: PLR0124: Extend `comparison-with-itself` to detect attribute, subscript, and call expressions
body:
### Summary

`PLR0124` currently only flags self-comparisons involving simple names (e.g., `a == a`). It does not detect self-comparisons with attribute access, subscripts, or call expressions. These are common copy-paste mistakes that can introduce subtle bugs.

## Example

[Playground | Ruff](https://play.ruff.rs/)

```python
# ✅ Detected by PLR0124
if a == a: ...
if left_count < left_count: ...

# ❌ Not detected by PLR0124
if self.x == self.x: ...
if slim_info.structure_id == slim_info.structure_id: ...
if a[0] == a[0]: ...
if obj.method() == obj.method(): ...
```

| Pattern | Example | Detected |
|---------|---------|:--------:|
| Simple name | `a == a` | ✅ |
| Simple name + other operators | `left_count < left_count` | ✅ |
| Attribute access | `self.x == self.x` | ❌ |
| Nested attribute | `slim_info.structure_id == slim_info.structure_id` | ❌ |
| Subscript | `a[0] == a[0]` | ❌ |
| Call | `obj.method() == obj.method()` | ❌ |

## Motivation

We encountered real bugs in production where a developer wrote something like:

```python
if slim_info.structure_id == slim_info.structure_id:
    do_something()
```

This was a copy-paste error — the developer intended to compare two different objects. The condition is always `True`, silently breaking the logic. `PLR0124` did not catch it because it only checks `Name` nodes.

## Suggested enhancement

It would be great if `PLR0124` could recursively compare AST nodes for structural equality, covering at least:

- `Attribute` — `self.x == self.x`, `a.b.c == a.b.c`
- `Subscript` — `a[0] == a[0]`, `d["key"] == d["key"]`
- `Call` — `obj.method() == obj.method()`

For `Call` expressions, while functions with side effects could theoretically return different results, in practice `f() == f()` is almost always a copy-paste mistake. Rare legitimate cases can be suppressed with `# noqa`.

title: Suggest PEP 634 pattern (match/case) for repeated equality checks on the same variable
body:
### Summary

It would be great to include a rule that detects `if`/`elif` chains that repeatedly check the same variable, and suggests refactoring to `match`/`case`, introduced in Python 3.10 via PEP 634. This could avoid repeated evaluations of the same expression and reduces the risk of inconsistencies across branches.

Example (value comparisons):
```
if status == "open":
    ...
elif status == "closed":
    ...
elif status == "pending":
    ...
else:
    ...
```
could be refactored to:
```
match status:
    case "open":
        ...
    case "closed":
        ...
    case "pending":
        ...
    case _:
        ...
```
Other common patterns that should be covered:

**Type checks**
```
if isinstance(x, A):
    ...
elif isinstance(x, B):
    ...
```
**None checks**
```
if x is None:
    ...
elif x == "a":
    ...
```
The detection logic should align with existing rules (e.g. `PLR1714` or `RET`,  detecting patterns with repeated `if` branches in case of “superfluous else” usages). An automated fix could be implemented as well which could be classified as safe for simple equality comparisons or unsafe for more complex patterns, as usage of `match/case` could change runtime behavior in some cases.

title: B018 does not trigger on dictionary subscript
body:
### Summary

I would have expected useless subscripts to get flagged the same way as useless attribute access, but it currently isn't the case:
```py
x.attr  # B018
x["item"]  # no error
```

In case you're wondering, this would have prevented a real bug. In a codebase, I found some code that looks like:
```py

+my_dictionary["yet_another_long_key"]
-my_dictionary["again_another_key"]
```
The intention was clearly to assign the result of the operations to `my_value`, but, due to missing parentheses, only the first term is assigned and the following 2 lines are useless expressions.

I do realize there could be some corner cases where `__getitem__` has a side-effect, though I believe the [caveats in the B018 documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/useless-expression/#known-problems) apply here as well and an explicit ignore/assignment is warranted. The same could be said about `__pos__` and `__neg__`, though they don't prevent an expression from being flagged:
```py
+x  # B018
-x  # B018
```

title: Consider improving `SIM102` and `SIM114` fixes
body:
I originally posted this in https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/23879#issuecomment-4033002209, but these rules look quite compelling on paper (in the documentation), where they suggest diffs like this:

SIM102:

```diff
-if foo:
-    if bar:
-        ...
+if foo and bar:
+    ...
```

SIM114:

```diff
-if x == 1:
-    print("Hello")
-elif x == 2:
+if x == 1 or x == 2:
     print("Hello")
```

However, in more complicated and maybe realistic scenarios, the fix can be less readable:

SIM114:

```diff
-if something in [value1, value2] and another > condition:
-    do_something()
-elif something_else == "a string" and condition:
+if something in [value1, value2] and another > condition or something_else == "a string" and condition:
     do_something()
```

This also makes you think about precedence, and it gets reformatted like this:

```py
if (
    something in [value1, value2]
    and another > condition
    or something_else == "a string"
    and condition
):
    do_something()
```

SIM102 can have the same effect:

```diff
-if something in [value1, value2] and another > condition:
-    if something_else == "a string" and condition:
-        do_something()
+if something in [value1, value2] and another > condition and something_else == "a string" and condition:
+    do_something()
```

(Note that SIM102 checks the `line-length` setting before suggesting this fix, so I ran with `--line-length=180`, if you have trouble reproducing)

One suggestion on #23879 was to make the precedence clear by inserting parentheses in the fixed code. I think another possibility could be not applying the rules to compound conditions, but that might be more controversial.

import sys

import click

    """Lorem ipsum.
    \f

    """
    print(bar)

13 | |         bar: This is documentation relevant to using foo from Python directly.

title: SIM105 should be suppressed for `except*` in Python 3.11
body:
### Summary

The fix for [`suppressible-exception` (SIM105)](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/suppressible-exception/) can change the program’s behavior in Python 3.11 for `except*`. If some code uses `except*`, it’s probably because a `BaseExceptionGroup` can be raised. Because `contextlib.suppress` only gained support for `BaseExceptionGroup` in Python 3.12, the fix is most likely wrong for `except*` in Python 3.11. SIM105 should be suppressed in that case: not just the fix, but the whole rule, because there’s generally no way to simplify the code under these circumstances, so it’s not helpful for Ruff to flag it at all. [Example](https://play.ruff.rs/6a83bee0-9697-4ad8-97aa-ce58e0761520):

body:
### Summary

Hi! Last week, PR #23537 added checks for "D420", sections order in docstrings. It seems like the implemented expected order for numpy-style is different than what the source, `numpydoc` does. 

I got an issue in a class docstring looking like this:

```
class Example:
    """
    An example class.

    Methods
    -------
    a_method

    Examples
    --------
    An example.
```

`ruff` says :  `D420 Section "Examples" appears after section "Methods" but should be before it`
`numpydoc` say : `GL07 Sections are in the wrong order. Correct order is: Methods, Examples`

`ruff` implements the correct order here : https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/f8b0b0fc1531cc92b78635f37f183cbdcb1cd537/crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/pydocstyle/rules/sections.rs#L2176-L2193

Most of the list is in the same order, but `ruff`'s last two elements "Methods" and "Attributes" are much higher in the list from `numpydoc`. This simply looks like an oversight, because it doesn't make much sense to document those at the end. Also, those are probably rarely used, which might explain why the issue was not seen in the original PR.

Here, I am assuming that `numpydoc` is the "authoritative" source for the order, I might be wrong.

title: A new rule to check literal arguments in `setuptools.setup(...)`
body:
### Summary

As the `pyproject.toml` specification becomes the standard recommendation, static metadata configurations should be moved from arguments in `setuptools.setup(...)` to `pyproject.toml`.

## Proposed Functionalities

Implement checks for literal argument values within `setuptools.setup(...)`:
- Identify parameters that correspond to static metadata fields defined in [PEP 621](https://peps.python.org/pep-0621/). If such values are static literals, emit a lint warning suggesting migration to `pyproject.toml`.
- Alternatively, enforce a strict rule that prohibits static literal values for these parameters in `setuptools.setup(...)`, emitting an error instead of a warning.

## Edge Cases

Handling files containing multiple `setuptools.setup(...)` calls across different logic branches:
- **Consistency Check**: Compare arguments assigned to the same parameters across branches. If values differ, the metadata is dynamic; thus, no migration warning should be issued.
- **Exemption Strategy**: Automatically suppress lint warnings for any file detected to have multiple `setuptools.setup(...)` calls, assuming potential dynamic behavior.

title: proposal: inclusive language rules for speciesist terminology
body:
## Proposal

Add inclusive language rules to Ruff that detect speciesist terminology in comments, docstrings, and string literals, suggesting clearer alternatives.

## Context

Ruff already covers code style, security, complexity, and typing. Inclusive language scanning is a natural extension — several other linting tools have added this category:
- ESLint: [eslint-plugin-speciesism](https://github.com/Open-Paws/eslint-plugin-speciesism)
- proselint: [PR #1483](https://github.com/amperser/proselint/pull/1483) — merged speciesism checks alongside existing sexism/LGBTQ+ checks
- woke: [PR #284](https://github.com/get-woke/woke/pull/284)
- alex/retext-equality: [PR #130](https://github.com/retextjs/retext-equality/pull/130)

## Example Rules

| Code | Rule | Fix |
|------|------|-----|
| `# Kill two birds with one stone` | `SPE001` | `# Accomplish two things at once` |
| `# This is a guinea pig feature` | `SPE002` | `# This is a test feature` |
| `# Treat servers like cattle, not pets` | `SPE003` | `# Treat servers as ephemeral, not persistent` |
| `CANARY_DEPLOYMENT = True` | `SPE004` | `PROGRESSIVE_ROLLOUT = True` |

## Severity

These would be `suggestion`-level rules, disabled by default, opt-in via configuration. Similar to how Ruff handles style preferences — available for teams that want them, invisible to those who don't.

## Academic Foundation

- Hagendorff et al. (2023). "Speciesist bias in AI." *AI and Ethics*.
- Takeshita et al. (2022). *Information Processing & Management*.
- Leach et al. (2023). *British Journal of Social Psychology*.

## Willingness to Contribute

Happy to implement if there's interest. [Open Paws](https://openpaws.ai) has already built speciesist language detection for 7+ tools.

Let's say I have

return 789

It appears that using a `Callable` (defined as a class with a `__call__` method) as a FastAPI dependency produces false positive `FAST003` errors: path parameters that are declared in the `__call__` method signature are not properly recognized.

This is demonstrated in the following example:

# main.py

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends
from typing import Annotated

app = FastAPI()


class Query:
    def __call__(self, id: str):
        pass


@app.get("/things/{id}")
async def get(thing: Annotated[str, Depends(Query)]):

Found 1 error.
No fixes available (1 hidden fix can be enabled with the `--unsafe-fixes` option).

By contrast, using a regular function as the dependency does not produce a false positive:
